# ARGUS 2027 build progress

The build session's log. Feature and gate status live in `docs/build/features.json`; read them with `python3 tools/build_ledger.py summary`. The live copies of both files are on the integration branch `platform/build-2027`; `main` keeps the starting copies until the build ends. How the session works is in `docs/build/SESSION.md`.

## Decisions made during the build

Choices the specs did not settle, with the reason. Newest first.

| Date | Feature | Decision | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2026-11-18 | FND-02 | The adapter guards what it gives the 2026 missions: `detector` has no default; it stays silent while any other node publishes the 2026 target topic; a `bullseye` under `min_score` (new parameter, 0.25, the 2026 detector's own `min_detection_confidence`) or centred outside the image is "nothing found"; a set stamped more than 0.1 s ahead of the adapter's clock is not passed on. It does not serve `/drone_package_drop/set_target_cv_enabled`, which the 2026 missions wait for: the detector it adapts has to | flight-guardian: two publishers on the mission's topic would let an older "found" overwrite a newer "not found"; 2026 never showed the missions a detection under 0.25; and the missions' staleness test is one-sided, so a stamp from another time base would never go stale. Whether a contract-only detector serves the enable service is that detector's design (CEN-13) |
| 2026-11-18 | FND-02 | With `features.detection_contract` on, the contract message is published after the two 2026 topics, and if its set-up fails (for instance `vision_msgs` is not installed) the node logs an error and runs as the 2026 detector | flight-guardian: the missions wait on this node's enable service, so it has to start whatever happens to the new output, and what they fly on should not wait for the box to be computed |
| 2026-11-18 | FND-02 | The 2026 YOLO node (`vision_pipeline/yolo_node.py`) is not put on the contract. It keeps publishing `Detection2DArray` with its model's numeric class ids on `/drone_control/detection`, which `mission_logger` reads | Its class ids are whatever the 2026 weights were trained with, and there is no 2027 model to map them to the contract's names (the training-data hold). LOC-5 replaces the node with one on the contract and DAT-01 fixes the names; `decode` refuses a numeric id until then |
| 2026-11-18 | FND-02 | The contract's code is `drone_mission_core/detection_contract.py` (no ROS): the class list, `topic_for`, `encode` and `decode` to and from `vision_msgs/Detection2DArray`, `scale_to_full_resolution`, and the 2026 point. Choices the spec leaves open: one hypothesis per detection; a frame with nothing found is published as an empty array with the frame's stamp; a detector's name is lower case letters, digits and underscores; `decode` refuses anything else (unknown class, score outside 0 to 1, a box of no size, no frame id) | One module every detector and every reader uses, so the vocabulary cannot drift. An empty array tells the estimator the detector looked and saw nothing, which silence does not. It is in the core package because the estimator (FND-06) and the missions read it there |
| 2026-11-18 | FND-02 | The 2026 detector joins the contract behind the node flag `features.detection_contract` (default false, declared in the five params files). With it on, `target_cv` also publishes `/perception/target_cv/detections`, class `bullseye`, with the image's stamp and frame id; it still publishes the two 2026 topics itself, unchanged. The contract's modules and `vision_msgs` are imported only with the flag on, and a failure on the contract side is caught so the 2026 topics still go out | Flags off the node must be the 2026 node, down to what it imports. The contract stamp is always the image's stamp, whatever `features.stamp_from_image` says, because the contract says so |
| 2026-11-18 | FND-02 | The adapter is a separate small node, `detection_legacy_adapter` (`drone_target_cv/legacy_adapter.py`), that turns any detector's contract topic back into `/drone_package_drop/target_detection` and `/drone_package_drop/image_size`. Nothing shipped starts it, and it must not run beside `target_cv`, which publishes those topics itself. Its `z` is the box's area, not the red area in pixels that 2026 puts there | The spec's sentence is "stays alive through a small adapter so the flags-off path is untouched". Flags off, the untouched path is the 2026 detector publishing the 2026 topic. The adapter is for the detectors that only speak the contract (the ring fit of CEN-13, the sim's oracle), so the 2026 missions can fly on them. A box does not carry the red area, and no mission reads `z` |
| 2026-11-18 | FND-02 | The box for the 2026 bullseye is the extent of the red pixels of the target the detector chose; its centre is the detector's own centre, which is not always the middle of that box. The pixels are those of the image the detector was given, and the frame id is the image's. In the sim that is Gazebo's `downcam_link` at 640 x 360; on the aircraft the 2026 grabbers send `camera_link` and a reduced image | The 2026 detector has no box of its own. "Full-resolution calibrated image" and "optical frame" are properties of the driver, and they hold when `argus_camera` is the driver (PLT-07), as with FND-01's capture time. A reader that needs them checks the frame id against the robot description |
| 2026-11-18 | FND-01 | On the aircraft a detection carries a capture time only when `argus_camera` is the camera driver (with `legacy_topics:=true` for the 2026 detector) and GStreamer's bindings are installed. No flight launch starts it yet; PLT-07's bringup does that. Until then `features.stamp_from_image` on a 2026 launch copies the 2026 grabber's stamp, which is its publish time, not a capture time | The 2026 grabbers are the fallback and are not changed. This narrows what FND-03's row below promised ("until FND-01 makes it the capture time"): FND-01 makes it so in the new driver, and the launch that uses the new driver is PLT-07's |
| 2026-11-18 | FND-01 | `capture_offset_s` is stored per sensor mode, not once per camera | The delay between exposure and the buffer's timestamp can differ between the 4K and the 720p60 mode of the same sensor, so the probe measures it in each |
| 2026-11-18 | FND-01 | `capture_clock.py` is in `argus_camera`, not a `cv/` folder. The CSI path that uses it (`GstCsiSource`) needs GStreamer's Python bindings (`gi`), imported inside a guard, and is chosen with `csi_backend:=gstreamer`; the default stays `opencv`, whose frames are stamped when read and say so (`stamp_source: read`). `gstreamer` without the bindings is an error | PLT-03's spec puts capture timestamps in the camera package. OpenCV's capture does not expose the pipeline's clock or base time, so a PTS read through it cannot be turned into a capture time; the bindings are a system package, which the session does not install. Which path flies must not depend on what happens to be installed on one Jetson, and the PTS path has only run against stand-ins (flight-guardian), so it is opt-in until the bench has seen it |
| 2026-11-18 | FND-01 | A buffer timestamp more than 2 ms in the future, or missing, is not used: the frame is stamped at the read and the fallback is counted. A frame more than 1 s old by its own timestamp is dropped and counted. The USB camera's time is read through OpenCV's `CAP_PROP_POS_MSEC` and taken to be the kernel's monotonic time. `capture_offset_s` cannot be negative | A wrong stamp presented as a capture time is worse than an honest read time, and an old frame restamped at the read would look fresh to the target timeout and to the stale-data guard (flight-guardian). Whether the OV9782's driver stamps on the monotonic clock is a bench question; if it does not, the checks turn its frames into counted fallbacks or drops, not wrong stamps |
| 2026-11-18 | FND-01 | FND-01's flag for "every downstream message copies the image's stamp" is the detector's node flag `features.stamp_from_image` (added under FND-03, default false). With it on the detection, the not-found detection and the image-size message all carry the image's stamp. A test fails if the 2027 detector, the YOLO node or the mission logger sets a stamp from its own clock | One flag for one behaviour. The YOLO node and the mission logger already copy the source stamp. The 2026 grabbers are where a stamp is born and are untouched, as is `vision_pipeline/target_cv.py`, the 2026 copy of the detector |
| 2026-11-18 | FND-01 | The sim line "frame stamp vs Gazebo render time within one frame period" is checked by `sim/time_check.py` in every sim-time flight: the 95th percentile of sim clock minus frame stamp, at receipt, must be within 33.3 ms, and where the scenario turns `stamp_from_image` on, at least 99% of detections must carry a frame's stamp | In the sim the stamp is Gazebo's render time by construction; what can go wrong is a node in between restamping, which this catches. One detection per mission (the "not found" sent on switching off) has no image |
| 2026-11-18 | FND-01 | `capture_offset_s` is 0 for every mode until the LED probe (PLT-05) measures it | The ledger note for this row: "PLT-05 supplies the measured camera offset later (default 0 until then)" |
| 2026-11-18 | FND-04 | The pose buffer is built and fed behind the existing mission flag `use_frame_time_pose` (declared false in all ten sequences). On its own the flag only keeps the history; nothing reads it until FND-05 and FND-07, which use the same flag unless their own spec work says otherwise | The spec names no flag. That one was declared for exactly this (the pose at frame time) and read by nothing |
| 2026-11-18 | FND-04 | `pose_at(stamp_ns)` takes a Python `int` of nanoseconds on the clock of MAVROS's header stamps and returns `PoseAt(stamp_ns, position, orientation, extrapolated)`. Anything else (a float, a numpy integer) gets None, and `add_pose` refuses such a stamp. Callers convert with `int()` | Nanosecond integers compare exactly and are what ROS stamps are; float seconds at wall-clock size lose a quarter of a microsecond. A numpy integer silently accepted in one place and not another would be worse than a clear rule |
| 2026-11-18 | FND-04 | Past the newest sample the buffer also answers None when there are not two poses at least 10 ms and at most 0.12 s apart to take the turn from, or no velocity stamped at or before the newest pose and within 0.12 s of it. Position is carried on by the reported velocity, attitude by the turn between those two poses | The spec says "using velocity" and "never falls back to the latest pose". `velocity_local` gives linear velocity only, so the turn comes from the poses themselves; a velocity from another moment, or a turn rate taken from two poses 3 ms apart, would be a guess presented as a pose (flight-guardian) |
| 2026-11-18 | FND-04 | Velocity comes from `/mavros/local_position/velocity_local` (east, north, up); angular rate is not kept. A gap of exactly 0.12 s is still interpolated and exactly 30 ms ahead still answered; a stamp equal to a stored sample returns that sample | It is the same MAVLink message as the pose, so it arrives at the same rate with the same stamps. The spec says "exceeds" and "at most" |
| 2026-11-18 | FND-04 | Samples may arrive a little out of order. One stamped more than 0.12 s before the newest is ignored; three such in a row are taken as the clock having stepped back, and the history is dropped and started again | Sorting a backward-stepped clock's samples in among the old ones would let `pose_at` blend two timelines and call it valid; refusing them for good would leave the buffer dead until the clock caught up (flight-guardian). FND-03's guard reports the step itself |
| 2026-11-18 | FND-04 | The buffer lives in the executor, with its own subscriptions beside the executor's 2026 pose callback. Another node that needs pose history calls `attach_pose_buffer` itself. Teammate issue #4 was checked on 17 and 18 Nov: no open pull request and nothing on `main` | Decision 2 of the brief: the estimator runs inside the executor and reads the pose at capture time without a ROS hop |

| 2026-11-18 | PLT-06 | The keeper requests every rate once on connection, and again only after a reboot (MAVROS reconnecting, or the flight controller's clock going back by more than 1 s) or when the rate it measures for a message is under 80% of what was asked over 5 s. It sends nothing while a mission is in a release or actuation state (the takeoff, the final column and the release itself), which it learns from the missions' `State: OLD -> NEW` lines on `/rosout`; the hold lapses if the executor is silent for 60 s. One request at a time through `/mavros/cmd/command`; 5 s of silence after a failure; a message still low after three accepted requests is left alone until it arrives at its rate or the next reboot. This replaces the 10 s repeat | The lead's instruction of 18 Nov: the repeat put a request in MAVROS's command queue every 10 s for the whole flight, and one that was not acknowledged could delay a gripper release by up to 5 s. Measured rates also catch what the repeat was for (the takeoff service's request for all streams at 20 Hz, and a reboot the sim does not show). The log is used for the mission state because it needs no change to the 2026 executor or missions; a test drives the real missions and fails if their state lines or names change. In the flight on this code the keeper sent 10 requests in all, against about 130 before |
